report.tagline: An app that delivers groceries and thousands of everyday items to your door in about 10 minutes.
report.simpleSummary: You open the Blinkit app, add milk, chips, a phone charger or a birthday gift, and pay. A rider brings it in about 10 minutes. This works because Blinkit keeps small warehouses, called dark stores, very close to where people live. It is owned by Eternal, the company that also owns Zomato, and it is now the biggest part of that company.

overview.whatItDoes: Blinkit sells groceries, fruits and vegetables, snacks, beauty, toys, electronics, stationery and gifts, and delivers them in about 10 minutes. It started as Grofers in 2013, switched to 10-minute delivery in 2021, and was bought by Zomato in 2022. Its founder, Albinder Dhindsa, became CEO of the whole Eternal group in early 2026.
howItWorks: Blinkit runs dark stores: small warehouses, closed to walk-in shoppers, each serving homes within about 2 to 3 km.
When you order, a picker in the store collects your items in about 2 minutes and packs them.
A delivery partner on a bike picks up the bag and rides a short distance to you, so most orders arrive in 8 to 15 minutes.
Bigger mother warehouses refill the dark stores every day, so popular items stay in stock.
Since late 2025 Blinkit buys and owns much of its stock (inventory model) instead of only letting sellers list items, which gives it more control over price and availability.
Brands pay Blinkit to show their products higher in search and on the home screen.
overview.valueProposition: Get almost anything you forgot or suddenly need, in minutes, without leaving home, at prices close to the local shop.

painPoints.howSolved: Order just that one item and get it in about 10 minutes.

painPoints.pain: Wasting time in traffic and queues for weekly shopping
painPoints.howSolved: Full grocery baskets arrive at home; past orders can be repeated in a few taps.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shows a delivery time (like 9 minutes) on top of the app based on your nearest store.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Speed is the main promise. It turns Blinkit into a habit for small, frequent orders.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Electronics, beauty, toys, kitchenware, pet care, stationery and even gaming consoles.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: More categories mean bigger baskets and more reasons to open the app, which helps cover the fixed cost of each store.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shows items you buy often and suggests add-ons at checkout.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Makes repeat orders fast and raises the average bill size.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shows the picker packing, then the rider on a map, with a live time count.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Builds trust in the 10-minute promise and cuts 'where is my order' calls.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Brands pay to appear at the top of search results and category pages.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Ads are high-margin money that helps Blinkit stay profitable even with low delivery fees.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Bistro is a separate app for 10-minute snacks and meals; Blinkit also offers printouts and has tried a 10-minute ambulance in Gurugram.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Uses the same dark-store and rider network for new needs, testing how far 'in minutes' can go.

Milk, diapers, fruits and atta added in a few taps.

userJourneys.persona: Student or bachelor in a hostel or PG

Finds chargers from 2 or 3 brands with prices.

businessModel.summary: Blinkit makes money in four ways: the margin on goods it sells, ad money from brands, fees from customers, and commissions from outside sellers. It spends most of that on riders, dark-store rent and staff, and discounts. Today it keeps less than ₹1 of profit for every ₹100 of goods sold.

revenueStreams.detail: Blinkit buys stock and sells it at a higher price (inventory model), or takes a cut from sellers who list on it. This is the biggest stream.
Brands pay for top spots in search and on the home screen. Ads are a few percent of order value but almost all of it is profit.
Delivery fee on small orders, a handling fee per order, small cart fee, and sometimes a rain or late-night surge fee.
Bistro food orders, print orders and other add-on services; small today.

businessModel.pricing: Products sold at or below MRP. Customer fees change by city and time. Typically: free delivery above a basket limit (often around ₹199), delivery fee around ₹25 to ₹30 below it, a small handling fee of a few rupees, and extra small-cart, rain or late-night fees at times. Exact fees not public and keep changing.
costDrivers: Last-mile delivery: paying riders per order, plus extra during rain and peak hours
Dark-store rent, power and cold storage
Store staff who pick and pack each order
Discounts and marketing to fight Zepto, Instamart, Flipkart Minutes and Amazon Now
Wastage of fruits, vegetables and dairy that expire
Opening new stores, which lose money for their first few months
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a rough ₹650 order (estimate). Blinkit keeps about ₹120 to ₹130 from product margin, ads and fees, which is its take rate (the share of each order it keeps as revenue) of roughly 19-20%. It spends about ₹45 to ₹50 on the rider, ₹30 on store rent and staff, ₹15 on warehousing, and ₹20 or more on discounts and other costs. That leaves a small contribution margin (money left after the direct costs of an order) of roughly ₹15 to ₹25. After office and tech costs, Blinkit's adjusted EBITDA was under 1% of order value in mid-2026, so about ₹5 on that order. Mature cities like Delhi-NCR earn over 5%, while new stores lose money, so profit depends on how fast new stores fill up with orders.

howTheyGetUsers: Opening new dark stores in new neighbourhoods and smaller cities; each new store makes 10-minute delivery possible for thousands of new homes
Word of mouth and social media posts about the speed
Festival and event moments like Diwali, Holi, IPL and Valentine's Day with special categories
whatBringsUsersBack: Speed builds a habit: once you get an item in 10 minutes, you stop making the trip to a shop
Order Again list makes repeat buying very fast
More categories mean more reasons to open the app each week
Free delivery above a basket limit pushes people to add more and come back often
Push notifications for deals and new launches
growth.moat: Blinkit has the most dark stores in the best locations, more orders per store than rivals, and a large ad business from brands. More orders per store make each store cheaper to run, so Blinkit can keep fees low while staying profitable. A rival would need years and thousands of crores to build the same store network and demand.

competitors.name: Zepto
competitors.positioning: Fast-growing 10-minute app, strong in metros, with Zepto Cafe for food.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Blinkit is bigger (917 million vs 640 million orders in FY26) and profitable at the EBITDA level, while Zepto still lost over ₹1,200 crore in Q4 FY26.

competitors.name: Swiggy Instamart
competitors.positioning: Quick commerce inside the Swiggy super-app, sold with Swiggy One membership.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Blinkit does about twice Instamart's orders and earns a profit, while Instamart loses money. Instamart benefits from Swiggy's food users.

competitors.name: Flipkart Minutes
competitors.positioning: Flipkart's 10-minute delivery service using its huge e-commerce brand and supply chain.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Blinkit has a head start in stores and daily habit; Flipkart has deeper pockets from Walmart and a bigger range for planned purchases.

competitors.name: Amazon Now and BigBasket BB Now
competitors.positioning: Amazon's fast-delivery push and Tata's BigBasket quick service.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Blinkit is built only for speed, so its store network is denser; Amazon and BigBasket are stronger in planned, bigger shopping.

competitors.name: Local kirana stores
competitors.positioning: Neighbourhood shops with credit, personal service and free home delivery.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Blinkit offers far more products and a live app; the kirana offers trust, credit and no fees.

northStar.metric: Orders delivered on time and complete per week (in 15 minutes or less, with no missing or damaged items)
northStar.why: It counts only orders where the customer got what they wanted, fast. This captures Blinkit's real promise, and more such orders also means busier stores and better profit.

strengths: Market leader with the largest dark-store network and the highest orders per store
First in the sector to reach EBITDA profit, which lets it invest without raising fresh money
Strong brand ad business that adds high-margin money
Fast expansion beyond groceries into electronics, gifting and premium products
Backed by Eternal's cash and Zomato's customer base; its founder now runs the whole group
weaknesses: Profit margin is still very thin, under 1% of order value
Heavy dependence on gig riders whose costs and protests can hit service
Fees and pricing have drawn public criticism and 'dark pattern' claims
New stores in smaller cities lose money at first and orders there are smaller
risks: Price war from Zepto, Instamart, Flipkart Minutes and Amazon Now with deep discounts
Rules on dark stores, FDI in inventory-led retail and gig worker welfare (social security codes)
Pushback from kirana and trader groups who say quick commerce kills small shops
Food safety raids and licence suspensions at dark stores
Customers getting tired of paying extra fees and returning to local shops
userComplaints: Surge, rain, handling and small cart fees that inflate the final bill
Prices sometimes higher than MRP or than the same item at a local shop
Expired, near-expiry or damaged products, especially dairy and fruits
Missing free items or missing items in the bag, with slow customer support
Delivery much slower than 10 minutes during rain and late nights

improvementIdeas.idea: Show all fees upfront on the home screen and offer one flat 'all-in' price option
improvementIdeas.problem: Users feel cheated by fees revealed only at checkout.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Fewer abandoned carts at checkout and less negative social media; better trust.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Checkout drop-off rate and fee-related complaints per 1,000 orders

improvementIdeas.idea: Freshness guarantee with expiry date shown on the product page and an instant refund button
improvementIdeas.problem: Complaints about expired dairy and spoiled fruits.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Higher trust for fresh categories, more weekly grocery baskets.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Fresh-category repeat rate and freshness complaint rate

improvementIdeas.idea: Scheduled 'next-morning' slot at lower fees for planned baskets
improvementIdeas.problem: Not every order needs 10 minutes; peak-hour orders strain riders.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Smooths demand, lowers rider cost per order and wins planned grocery shopping from BigBasket and Amazon.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Share of orders in scheduled slots and cost per order

improvementIdeas.idea: Smart store stocking for smaller cities based on local searches with zero results
improvementIdeas.problem: Tier-2 users find a smaller range and leave.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: More orders per new store and faster path to profit.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Zero-result search rate and orders per store per day in new cities

improvementIdeas.idea: Rain mode: warn users of delays upfront and give a small credit if late
improvementIdeas.problem: Missed delivery times during rain hurt the core promise.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Better satisfaction even when late; fewer support tickets.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: On-time rate in rain hours and CSAT on late orders

pmLessons: Speed can be a product. Blinkit did not invent groceries online, it made them fast enough to change habits.
Fixed costs need volume. A dark store only makes money once it fills up with orders, so growth and profit are linked.
Ads can fund low prices. Brand ad money lets Blinkit keep customer fees low while still earning.
Expanding categories raises basket size, but each new category (like electronics) needs its own storage, returns and trust rules.
Fees are a product choice too. Too many small fees save margin but hurt trust.

interviewQuestions.question: Blinkit's orders are growing but users complain about fees. Would you remove the handling fee?
interviewQuestions.hint: Start with goals (trust vs margin). Size the fee's money impact per order. Test removal in a few cities and track checkout drop-off, order frequency and EBITDA per order before rolling out.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide which new category Blinkit should add next?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at zero-result searches, urgency of need, size and fragility of items, margin and ad potential, and return risk. Pick one, define success metrics, run a pilot in a few stores.

interviewQuestions.question: Orders in a new tier-2 city are lower than planned. How do you diagnose it?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split the funnel: awareness, installs, first orders, repeat orders, basket size. Compare with a similar metro launch. Check assortment, prices vs local shops, delivery time and payment options.

interviewQuestions.question: What should be Blinkit's north star metric and why?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick something that shows value to the user, like on-time and complete orders per week. Explain why GMV or revenue alone is weaker, then break it into drivers like customers, frequency and reliability.

interviewQuestions.question: Zepto launches heavy discounts in Mumbai. How should Blinkit respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Do not match blindly. Look at which users are switching, protect loyal users with targeted offers, lean on speed and range, and set a spending limit tied to retention gains.

assumptions: The ₹650 order size and the cost split in unit economics are estimates built from reported margins, not company-published numbers.
Market share of about 45-50% is an analyst-style estimate; Blinkit does not publish market share.
Fee levels (delivery fee around ₹25 to ₹30, free above about ₹199) vary by city and time and are based on user reports.
Daily order figure is a simple average of the FY26 annual order count.
